Neonatal Weddell seals enter the world at a surprisingly modest size considering the formidable adult dimensions the species attains. At parturition, newborn pups typically measure 120 centimeters [Lb = 120 centimeters] in total length, while female neonates are only slightly smaller at approximately 118 centimeters [Lb = approximately 118 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at birth is substantial, with a mean value near 29,000 grams [Wwb = 29,000 grams], reflecting the extensive energy reserves deposited during the lengthy gestation period. This initial mass supports the neonate through the critical early days of maternal provisioning and rapid growth that characterize the suckling juvenile stage. The developmental chronology of these dependent young unfolds at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], under which weaning occurs 40 days after birth [tx = 40 days after birth]. This brief nursing interval, typical of phocid seals that exploit dense, lipid-rich milk, allows mothers to transfer a remarkable quantity of energy to their offspring before returning to foraging. The duration of maternal investment is comparatively short relative to other marine mammals of equivalent adult body size.

Adult body size in Leptonychotes weddellii exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females ultimately surpassing males in both length and mass. The maximum recorded total length for female adults reaches 277 centimeters [Li = 277 centimeters], whereas males attain a somewhat lesser ultimate length of 263 centimeters [Li = 263 centimeters]. This pattern of female-biased size is relatively uncommon among phocid seals and may relate to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation in the high-latitude Antarctic environment. Adult females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 348,000 grams [Wwi = 348,000 grams], a value consistent with the substantial blubber layer required for thermal insulation and energy storage during extended fasting periods associated with breeding. Males, in contrast, reach a maximum adult body mass of 322,000 grams [Wwi = 322,000 grams], their slightly lighter build possibly reflecting a different allocation of resources toward territorial defense and underwater vocal displays during the pupping season. These size differences are established gradually over several years of post-weaning growth and are maintained throughout the reproductively active adult phase.

The reproductive biology of the Weddell seal is characterized by a slow-paced life history optimized for the extreme seasonality of the Antarctic pack ice. Females deliver a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and the interval between successive pupping events averages 548 days [F_R_i = averages 548 days], a pattern that emerges under the thermal conditions of active metabolism maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This biennial or triennial reproductive frequency, recorded in several long-term studies, reflects the high energetic cost of lactation and the need to replenish body reserves before the next breeding attempt. The gestation period itself lasts 304 days [tg = 304 days] at the same core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a duration that includes a period of embryonic diapause common among pinnipeds. This delay between fertilization and implantation ensures that parturition coincides with the availability of stable ice platforms and adequate food resources for the subsequent nursing period. The temporal coordination of these reproductive events is critical for pup survival in the harsh Antarctic environment.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a protracted developmental trajectory, with males and females maturing at markedly different ages measured at the species' typical core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Female Weddell seals reach puberty at 1,365 days after birth [tp = 1,365 days after birth], a milestone that corresponds to approximately 3.7 years of age at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Males, by contrast, require considerably longer to attain reproductive maturity, with the onset of puberty occurring at 1,642 days after birth [tp = 1,642 days after birth], or roughly 4.5 years at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This delayed maturation in males is hypothesized to reflect the competitive demands of establishing a territory and the physical condition necessary for successful underwater vocal displays during the breeding season. The divergence in maturation schedules between the sexes is a common pattern among polygynous or promiscuous pinniped species and likely contributes to the observed skew in reproductive success among adult males. Following puberty, individuals enter the breeding adult mammal stage and may reproduce over several decades.

Longevity records for Weddell seals indicate a maximum lifespan of 25 years [am = 25 years] under the physiological conditions sustained at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This substantial lifespan relative to body size is characteristic of deep-diving marine mammals that exhibit low adult mortality rates and extended reproductive windows. At weaning, pups have already accumulated substantial body reserves, reaching a wet weight of 115,900 grams [Wwx = 115,900 grams] after the 40-day period of maternal investment. This represents a fourfold increase over the birth mass, a growth rate fueled entirely by the exceptionally lipid-rich milk produced by lactating females. The resorption of placental tissues and the clearance of foetal membranes are completed rapidly following parturition, allowing the neonate to focus on nursing and thermoregulation. As these weaned juveniles transition toward nutritional independence, they must learn to forage beneath the fast ice, a skill that requires both physical stamina and the ability to locate breathing holes in the rapidly changing Antarctic sea ice environment.
